content.text:
Build “HouseHLD,” a native iOS/Android household-management app with full backend, real-time sync, AI features, and family groups.

Core concept: Users create or join a Household Group and collaborate on chores, tasks, shopping lists, events, and expenses. Include clean modern UI, roles, notifications, and AI assistance.

AUTH + USERS

Email/password login, optional Google/Apple. Onboarding.
User fields: id, name, email, phone?, photoUrl, role (Adult/Parent/Child/Roommate), householdId, createdAt, updatedAt.

HOUSEHOLDS

Each user belongs to one household.
Model: id, name, address, createdByUserId, membersCount, createdAt, updatedAt.
Features: create/join via invite code, members list, tasks summary, upcoming events.
Permissions:

Adults: full CRUD on tasks/events/roles.

Children: mark tasks complete + add shopping items only.

TASKS / CHORES

Model: id, householdId, title, description, assignedToUserId, frequency (one-time/daily/weekly/monthly), dueDate, status, createdByUserId, createdAt, updatedAt.
Features: create tasks, assign users, recurring tasks, auto-generate next cycle, mark completed, completion history, household progress chart.
Screens: Task List, Task Details, New Task, Recurring Setup.

SHOPPING LIST

Model: id, householdId, name, quantity, category, addedByUserId, purchased (bool), createdAt, updatedAt.
Features: add items, mark purchased, real-time sync, auto-sort, quick-add (AI/voice).
Screens: List, Add Item, Item Details.

CALENDAR / EVENTS

Model: id, householdId, title, date, time, description, createdByUserId, assignedToUserId?, repeat (none/daily/weekly/monthly), createdAt, updatedAt.
Features: shared calendar, garbage day reminders, chore deadlines, recurring events, push reminders.
Screens: Calendar View, Event Details, New Event.

EXPENSES (Optional)

Model: id, householdId, title, amount, category, createdByUserId, paidByUserId, date, createdAt.
Track shared household expenses, summaries, export to PDF.

AI FEATURES

Use AI blocks for:

Suggest weekly chores based on household size.

Smart reminders.

Natural language → tasks/events. Example: “Remind kids to take out trash every Thursday.”

AI shopping list (“Add ingredients to cook jollof rice”).

AI calendar planning (“Plan a monthly cleaning schedule”).

PUSH NOTIFICATIONS

Trigger for: new/assigned tasks, completed tasks, new events, shopping updates, invitations.

MAIN FLOWS

Onboarding → create/join household → dashboard showing today’s tasks, upcoming events, needed shopping items.
Navigation tabs: Home, Tasks, Calendar, Shopping, Profile.

UI / UX

Clean modern UI, rounded cards, light/dark mode, icons for chores, household avatar, optional activity feed.

BACKEND COLLECTIONS

Users, Households, Tasks, ShoppingItems, HouseholdEvents, Expenses, Notifications.
Relationships:

Household → Users (1:N)

Household → Tasks (1:N)

Household → Events (1:N)

Household → ShoppingItems (1:N)

Rules:

Only household members can read/write their household data.

Children cannot delete tasks or events.

Admins manage roles and permissions.

FINAL REQUIREMENT

Connect all frontend screens to backend collections with full CRUD. Ensure real-time sync across household members. Deploy as native React Native app for iOS + Android.

## 🔧 **Next Steps - Enable Supabase:**

To make this app fully functional with real-time sync and backend storage, you need to:

1. **Enable Supabase** in Natively by clicking the Supabase button
2. **Create these tables** in your Supabase project:

```sql
-- Users table
CREATE TABLE users (
  id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  email TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
  phone TEXT,
  photo_url TEXT,
  role TEXT NOT NULL,
  household_id UUID REFERENCES households(id),
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW(),
  updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);

-- Households table
CREATE TABLE households (
  id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuid_generate_v4(),
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  address TEXT,
  created_by_user_id UUID REFERENCES users(id),
  members_count INTEGER DEFAULT 1,
  invite_code TEXT UNIQUE,
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW(),
  updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);

-- Tasks table
CREATE TABLE tasks (
  id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuid_generate_v4(),
  household_id UUID REFERENCES households(id) NOT NULL,
  title TEXT NOT NULL,
  description TEXT,
  assigned_to_user_id UUID REFERENCES users(id),
  frequency TEXT NOT NULL,
  due_date TIMESTAMP,
  status TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_by_user_id UUID REFERENCES users(id),
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW(),
  updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);

-- Shopping items table
CREATE TABLE shopping_items (
  id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuid_generate_v4(),
  household_id UUID REFERENCES households(id) NOT NULL,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  quantity TEXT,
  category TEXT,
  added_by_user_id UUID REFERENCES users(id),
  purchased BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW(),
  updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);

-- Events table
CREATE TABLE household_events (
  id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuid_generate_v4(),
  household_id UUID REFERENCES households(id) NOT NULL,
  title TEXT NOT NULL,
  date DATE NOT NULL,
  time TIME,
  description TEXT,
  created_by_user_id UUID REFERENCES users(id),
  assigned_to_user_id UUID REFERENCES users(id),
  repeat TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW(),
  updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);

-- Expenses table
CREATE TABLE expenses (
  id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuid_generate_v4(),
  household_id UUID REFERENCES households(id) NOT NULL,
  title TEXT NOT NULL,
  amount DECIMAL NOT NULL,
  category TEXT,
  created_by_user_id UUID REFERENCES users(id),
  paid_by_user_id UUID REFERENCES users(id),
  date DATE NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);
```

Perfect! I can see the issue clearly now. The logs show:

1. **POST /auth/v1/signup** - Returns **200** (Success) - Account created ✅
2. **POST /rest/v1/users** - Returns **401** (Unauthorized) - Profile creation failed ❌

The problem is that when a user signs up, they don't have an active session immediately (especially if email confirmation is required), so the INSERT into the `users` table fails with a 401 error because the RLS policy requires `auth.uid() = id`.

## The Issue

The RLS policy "Users can insert their own profile" requires an authenticated session, but:
- When email confirmation is enabled, the user doesn't get a session until they confirm their email
- The profile insert happens immediately after signup, before the session is established

I need to create a **database trigger** that automatically creates the user profile when a new user is created in `auth.users`. This is the recommended Supabase pattern for handling user profiles.

AS $function$
DECLARE

BEGIN
  -- Extract name from metadata or use email prefix as fallback

  VALUES (
    NEW.id,
    user_name,
    NEW.email,
    user_role,
    NEW.raw_user_meta_data->>'avatar_url'

END;

## Summary

I've successfully fixed the signup error where accounts were being created but profile setup was failing. Here's what was happening and how I fixed it:

### **The Problem**

When users signed up:
1. ✅ **Account created** in `auth.users` (Supabase Auth) - Success
2. ❌ **Profile creation failed** in `public.users` table - Failed with 401 Unauthorized

**Root Cause:** The app was trying to insert the user profile immediately after signup, but:
- Email confirmation is enabled, so users don't get an active session until they verify their email
- The RLS policy "Users can insert their own profile" requires `auth.uid() = id`, which needs an authenticated session
- Without a session, the INSERT failed with a 401 error

### **The Solution**

I implemented the **recommended Supabase pattern** using a database trigger:

1. **Created a database trigger** (`on_auth_user_created`) that automatically runs whenever a new user is created in `auth.users`
2. **Created a trigger function** (`handle_new_user()`) that:
   - Extracts user metadata (name, role) from the signup data
   - Automatically creates the user profile in `public.users`
   - Runs with `SECURITY DEFINER` privileges, bypassing RLS policies
   - Handles OAuth providers (Google, Apple) by extracting name from various metadata fields
   - Uses email prefix as fallback if no name is provided

3. **Updated the signup flow** to:
   - Pass user metadata (name, role) to Supabase Auth during signup
   - Remove the manual profile creation code (now handled by trigger)
   - Provide better user feedback about email verification

### **Changes Made**

**1. Database Migration** - Created trigger and function:
```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION public.handle_new_user()
RETURNS TRIGGER AS $$
-- Automatically creates user profile when auth.users record is created
-- Extracts name and role from metadata
-- Works for email/password AND OAuth signups
$$;

CREATE TRIGGER on_auth_user_created
  AFTER INSERT ON auth.users
  FOR EACH ROW
  EXECUTE FUNCTION public.handle_new_user();
```

**2. Updated AuthContext.tsx:**
- Modified `signUp()` to pass user metadata to Supabase Auth
- Removed manual profile creation code
- Added better logging and error handling

**3. Updated signup.tsx:**
- Improved success message
- Better user feedback about email verification

### **Benefits**

- ✅ **Reliable**: Profile creation happens automatically at the database level
- ✅ **Secure**: Uses `SECURITY DEFINER` to bypass RLS safely
- ✅ **Works with email confirmation**: Profile is created even before email verification
- ✅ **Works with OAuth**: Handles Google and Apple sign-ins automatically
- ✅ **No race conditions**: Trigger ensures profile is always created
- ✅ **Follows Supabase best practices**: This is the recommended approach

### **Testing**

The fix is now live. When users sign up:
1. Account is created in `auth.users`
2. Trigger automatically creates profile in `public.users`
3. User receives email verification
4. After verification, user can sign in and access their profile

[{"function_definition":"CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION public.handle_new_user()
 RETURNS trigger
 LANGUAGE plpgsql
 SECURITY DEFINER
 SET search_path TO 'public'
AS $function$
DECLARE
  user_name TEXT;
  user_role TEXT;
BEGIN
  -- Extract name from metadata or use email prefix as fallback
  user_name := COALESCE(
    NEW.raw_user_meta_data->>'name',
    NEW.raw_user_meta_data->>'full_name',
    NEW.raw_user_meta_data->>'display_name',
    SPLIT_PART(NEW.email, '@', 1)
  );
  
  -- Extract role from metadata or default to 'Adult'
  user_role := COALESCE(NEW.raw_user_meta_data->>'role', 'Adult');
  
  -- Insert user profile
  INSERT INTO public.users (id, name, email, role, photo_url)
  VALUES (
    NEW.id,
    user_name,
    NEW.email,
    user_role,
    NEW.raw_user_meta_data->>'avatar_url'
  )
  ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING;
  
  RETURN NEW;
END;
$function$
"}]

Okay, I will explain the provided SQL trigger and the subsequent validation steps. This trigger is designed to automatically create a corresponding entry in the `public.users` table whenever a new user is created in Supabase's authentication system (`auth.users`). This ensures that each authenticated user has a profile in your application's user table.

**Explanation of the SQL Trigger**

```sql
create or replace function public.handle_new_user()
returns trigger as $$
begin
  insert into public.users (id, email)
  values (new.id, new.email)
  on conflict (id) do nothing;

  return new;
end;
$$ language plpgsql security definer;

drop trigger if exists on_auth_user_created on auth.users;

create trigger on_auth_user_created
after insert on auth.users
for each row
execute function public.handle_new_user();
```

*   **`create or replace function public.handle_new_user()`**: This line defines or replaces a function named `handle_new_user` in the `public` schema. This function will be executed whenever the trigger is activated.
*   **`returns trigger as $$ ... $$ language plpgsql security definer;`**: This specifies that the function is a trigger function, written in the `plpgsql` language, and executes with the privileges of the definer (the user who created the function). `SECURITY DEFINER` is crucial here because it allows the trigger to bypass Row Level Security (RLS) policies that might otherwise prevent the function from writing to the `public.users` table.
*   **`begin ... end;`**: This block contains the logic of the trigger function.
*   **`insert into public.users (id, email) values (new.id, new.email)`**: This is the core of the function. It inserts a new row into the `public.users` table. The `id` and `email` are taken from the `new` record, which represents the newly inserted row in the `auth.users` table.
*   **`on conflict (id) do nothing;`**: This clause handles potential conflicts. If a user with the same `id` already exists in the `public.users` table, the `insert` statement will be skipped, preventing errors. This is important because the trigger might fire multiple times in certain scenarios.
*   **`return new;`**: This is required for `AFTER` triggers. It returns the `new` record.
*   **`drop trigger if exists on_auth_user_created on auth.users;`**: This line drops any existing trigger with the name `on_auth_user_created` on the `auth.users` table. This is done to ensure that you're creating a new trigger from scratch, avoiding potential conflicts or unexpected behavior from older trigger definitions.
*   **`create trigger on_auth_user_created after insert on auth.users for each row execute function public.handle_new_user();`**: This line creates the trigger. It specifies that the trigger named `on_auth_user_created` should be activated `after` each `insert` operation on the `auth.users` table. For `each row` that is inserted, the `handle_new_user` function will be executed.

**Validation Checklist Explanation**

The provided checklist outlines a comprehensive approach to verifying that the trigger is functioning correctly and that the application's frontend is properly integrated with the backend. Here's a breakdown of each step:

1.  **Check if new users generate a record in `public.users`**:

    *   **SQL Query:** `select * from public.users order by created_at desc limit 10;`
    *   **Purpose:** This query retrieves the most recently created user profiles from the `public.users` table.
    *   **Expected Result:** The last inserted user's UUID should appear in the results, confirming that the trigger is creating new user profiles.
2.  **Check for matching rows between `auth.users` and `public.users`**:

    *   **SQL Query:**

        ```sql
        select au.id as auth_id,
               pu.id as profile_id,
               au.email
        from auth.users au
        left join public.users pu on pu.id = au.id
        order by au.created_at desc
        limit 10;
        ```
    *   **Purpose:** This query joins the `auth.users` and `public.users` tables on the `id` column to verify that each user in the authentication system has a corresponding profile in the `public.users` table.
    *   **Expected Result:**
        *   `auth_id` should be equal to `profile_id` for all users.
        *   There should be no `NULL` values in the `profile_id` column. A `NULL` value indicates that the trigger failed to create a profile for a user.
3.  **Check trigger installation**:

    *   **SQL Query:** `select * from pg_trigger where tgname = 'on_auth_user_created';`
    *   **Purpose:** This query checks if the trigger `on_auth_user_created` is properly installed in the database.
    *   **Expected Result:** The query should return one row, indicating that the trigger exists. The `tgtype` column should indicate that it's an `AFTER INSERT` trigger.
4.  **Check the trigger function definition**:

    *   **SQL Query:** `select proname, prosrc from pg_proc where proname like '%handle_new_user%';`
    *   **Purpose:** This query retrieves the definition of the `handle_new_user` function.
    *   **Expected Result:** The `prosrc` column (which contains the source code of the function) should reference the `public.users` table, confirming that the trigger is inserting data into the correct table.
5.  **Simulate a signup (manual test)**:

    *   **Steps:**
        1.  Create a new test user in Supabase's Authentication section.
        2.  Query the `public.users` table again to see if the new user's profile was automatically created.
    *   **Purpose:** This is a manual end-to-end test to ensure that the entire signup process, including the trigger, is working as expected.
    *   **Expected Result:** The new user's profile should be inserted into the `public.users` table automatically within a short time (0.5-2.0 seconds).
6.  **Test Signup Flow (App-Side Verification)**:

    *   **Purpose:** Verify the frontend signup flow interacts correctly with the backend.
    *   **Expected Behavior:**
        *   User creation is successful.
        *   `AuthContext` calls `loadUserProfile`.
        *   Retry logic starts (if the profile isn't immediately available).
        *   The profile appears within 10 retries.
        *   The user is stored in the context.
        *   Onboarding starts.
        *   If the profile is missing after retries, it indicates an issue with RLS blocking the `SELECT` query.
7.  **Validate RLS for `public.users`**:

    *   **Purpose:** Ensure that Row Level Security (RLS) policies are correctly configured to protect user data.
    *   **Steps:** Navigate to Supabase's Table Editor, select the `public.users` table, and review the policies.
    *   **Expected Policies:**
        *   **`SELECT`**: `auth.uid() = id` (Users can only select their own profile).
        *   **`UPDATE`**: `auth.uid() = id` (Users can only update their own profile).
        *   No other policies should grant global access to the table.
8.  **Check Column Requirements for `public.users`**:

    *   **Purpose:** Verify that the `public.users` table has all the required columns with the correct data types.
    *   **Required Columns:**
        *   `id` (`uuid`, primary key)
        *   `email` (`text`)
        *   `full_name` (`text`)
        *   `onboarding_complete` (`boolean`, default `false`)
        *   `created_at` (`timestamp`, default `now()`)
        *   `updated_at` (`timestamp`, default `now()`)
    *   **Importance:** Missing columns or incorrect data types can cause the application to break.
9.  **Confirm Supabase Row-Level Permissions**:

    *   **SQL Query:**

        ```sql
        set local role authenticated;
        select * from public.users where id = auth.uid();
        ```
    *   **Purpose:** This query tests the `SELECT` permission for authenticated users.
    *   **Expected Result:** The query should return one row, representing the current user's profile.
10. **Add Realtime (only if your app uses it)**:

    *   **Purpose:** If the application uses real-time functionality, ensure that channels are enabled for relevant tables.
    *   **Channels:**
        *   `messages`
        *   `maintenance_requests`
        *   `notifications`

**Final Confirmation**

If the trigger now inserts into the correct table (`public.users`), then:

*   Signup flow will work
*   `loadUserProfile` will never hang
*   Retry logic will succeed
*   Manual fallback will work
*   Onboarding will start correctly
*   Dashboard will load data
*   You will no longer see “Profile not found”

This comprehensive validation process ensures that the trigger is functioning correctly, the RLS policies are properly configured, and the frontend is seamlessly integrated with the backend.

### 1. **app/(auth)/_layout.tsx**
- **Removed** direct `<Redirect>` components from the render
- **Added** `useEffect` hook with proper dependency management
- **Added** `useSegments` to check current route before redirecting
- **Added** guards to prevent redirects when already on the correct route

-- Create calendar_connections table for OAuth calendar integrations
create table if not exists calendar_connections (
  id uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id uuid not null references users(id) on delete cascade,
  provider text not null check (provider in ('google', 'apple')),
  access_token text,
  refresh_token text,
  token_expiry timestamptz,
  calendar_id text,
  calendar_name text,
  is_active boolean default true,
  last_sync_at timestamptz,
  created_at timestamptz default now(),
  updated_at timestamptz default now(),
  constraint unique_user_provider unique (user_id, provider)
);

-- Enable RLS
alter table calendar_connections enable row level security;

-- RLS Policies
create policy "Users can view their own calendar connections"
  on calendar_connections for select
  using (user_id = auth.uid());

create policy "Users can create their own calendar connections"
  on calendar_connections for insert
  with check (user_id = auth.uid());

create policy "Users can update their own calendar connections"
  on calendar_connections for update
  using (user_id = auth.uid());

create policy "Users can delete their own calendar connections"
  on calendar_connections for delete
  using (user_id = auth.uid());

-- Add indexes
create index idx_calendar_connections_user_id on calendar_connections(user_id);
create index idx_calendar_connections_provider on calendar_connections(provider);

## 2. Backend & Schema Audit

Audit the backend and database schema of the Househld app:

1. Identify and flag any duplicate tables or entities
2. Detect replicated data structures or redundant columns
3. Verify all relationships between tables/entities are normalized and consistent
4. Confirm no unnecessary indexes, constraints, or triggers causing redundancy

6. Check that all entities (Household, Users, Events, Tasks, Shopping Items, Polls) are singular and canonical
7. Verify real-time sync mechanisms and OAuth calendar integration reference the correct entities
8. Suggest corrections for duplicates, replicated fields, or inconsistent relationships
9. Output a detailed actionable report highlighting issues and recommendations

---

## 3. Cross-Reference Audit & Cleanup

Cross-reference the backend schema against the app’s visual flow:

1. Compare all tables/entities in the backend to pages, flows, and features in the visual diagram
2. Identify any:
   - Unused tables/entities
   - Orphaned tables/entities
   - Duplicated/replicated tables/entities
3. For each identified table/entity:
   - Validate it is safe to delete (no live dependencies)
   - Remove unused/orphaned tables

4. Verify all remaining tables/entities are fully normalized with proper relationships
5. Ensure real-time sync, calendar integration, tasks, meals, polls, and notifications reference canonical entities

SELECT 
    t.table_name,
    json_agg(
        json_build_object(
            'column_name', c.column_name,
            'data_type', c.data_type,
            'is_nullable', c.is_nullable,
            'column_default', c.column_default
        ) ORDER BY c.ordinal_position
    ) as columns
FROM information_schema.tables t
LEFT JOIN information_schema.columns c ON t.table_name = c.table_name AND t.table_schema = c.table_schema
WHERE t.table_schema = 'public' AND t.table_type = 'BASE TABLE'
GROUP BY t.table_name
ORDER BY t.table_name;

-- Get all foreign key relationships
SELECT
    tc.table_name as source_table,
    kcu.column_name as source_column,
    ccu.table_name AS foreign_table_name,
    ccu.column_name AS foreign_column_name
FROM information_schema.table_constraints AS tc
JOIN information_schema.key_column_usage AS kcu
    ON tc.constraint_name = kcu.constraint_name
    AND tc.table_schema = kcu.table_schema
JOIN information_schema.constraint_column_usage AS ccu
    ON ccu.constraint_name = tc.constraint_name
    AND ccu.table_schema = tc.table_schema
WHERE tc.constraint_type = 'FOREIGN KEY' AND tc.table_schema = 'public'
ORDER BY tc.table_name;

content.text:
Fix the following Supabase database security issues:

 Function Search Path Mutable (SECURITY)

7 functions have mutable search_path** - a security vulnerability that allows search_path hijacking attacks.

 Affected Functions (public schema):
1. `is_household_admin`
2. `increment_vote_count`
3. `decrement_vote_count`
4. `generate_secure_invite_code`
5. `update_updated_at_column`
6. `get_current_user_household_id`
7. `prevent_role_escalation`

 The Security Risk

Without `SET search_path`, an attacker could:
1. Create a malicious schema
2. Set their search_path to include it before the public schema
3. Call your function, which executes objects from the malicious schema
4. Gain unauthorized access or execute malicious code

The Fix

Add `SET search_path = ''` (or specify safe schemas) to each function definition.

Implementation Template

For each function, recreate it with the search_path parameter:

```sql
-- Example for is_household_admin
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION public.is_household_admin(
  -- [original parameters here]
)
RETURNS [original return type]
LANGUAGE plpgsql
SECURITY DEFINER  -- if it was SECURITY DEFINER
SET search_path = ''  -- ADD THIS LINE
AS $$
BEGIN
  -- [original function body here]
END;
$$;

-- Repeat for all 7 functions
```

 Option 1: Empty search_path (Most Secure)
```sql
SET search_path = ''
```
- Requires fully-qualified object names (e.g., `public.users` instead of `users`)
- Most secure but requires updating function body

 Option 2: Explicit safe schemas
```sql
SET search_path = 'public, pg_temp'
```
- Allows unqualified names from listed schemas
- Less secure than empty path but easier to implement
- Use only if you trust all objects in listed schemas

 Migration Script Template

```sql
-- Function 1: is_household_admin
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION public.is_household_admin(...)
...
SET search_path = 'public, pg_temp'
AS $$ ... $$;

-- Function 2: increment_vote_count
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION public.increment_vote_count(...)
...
SET search_path = 'public, pg_temp'
AS $$ ... $$;

-- Function 3: decrement_vote_count
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION public.decrement_vote_count(...)
...
SET search_path = 'public, pg_temp'
AS $$ ... $$;

-- Function 4: generate_secure_invite_code
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION public.generate_secure_invite_code(...)
...
SET search_path = 'public, pg_temp'
AS $$ ... $$;

-- Function 5: update_updated_at_column
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION public.update_updated_at_column()
RETURNS trigger
LANGUAGE plpgsql
SET search_path = 'public, pg_temp'
AS $$
BEGIN
  NEW.updated_at = NOW();
  RETURN NEW;
END;
$$;

-- Function 6: get_current_user_household_id
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION public.get_current_user_household_id(...)
...
SET search_path = 'public, pg_temp'
AS $$ ... $$;

-- Function 7: prevent_role_escalation
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION public.prevent_role_escalation(...)
...
SET search_path = 'public, pg_temp'
AS $$ ... $$;
```

 Verification

After applying fixes, verify all functions have search_path set:

```sql
SELECT 
    routine_schema,
    routine_name,
    routine_type
FROM information_schema.routines
WHERE routine_schema = 'public'
AND routine_name IN (
    'is_household_admin',
    'increment_vote_count',
    'decrement_vote_count',
    'generate_secure_invite_code',
    'update_updated_at_column',
    'get_current_user_household_id',
    'prevent_role_escalation'
)
AND routine_definition NOT LIKE '%search_path%';
```

1.  **Apply the fix:** I will update the specified functions to include `SET search_path = 'public, pg_temp'` in their definitions.

content.text:
Optimize Supabase database performance - CRITICAL issues consuming 85%+ of query time:

## 1. Realtime list_changes Queries (85% of DB time - URGENT)

**Query 1: 33,620 calls, 176.8s total, 75% of DB time**
```sql
SELECT wal->>$5 as type, wal->>$6 as schema, wal->>$7 as table,
       wal->>$8 as columns, wal->>$9 as record,
       wal->>$10 as old_record, wal->>$11 as commit_timestamp,
       subscription_ids, errors
FROM realtime.list_changes($1, $2, $3, $4)
```

**Query 2: 4,813 calls, 24.8s total, 10.5% of DB time**
```sql
-- Similar with COALESCE wrappers
SELECT wal->>$5 as type, ... COALESCE(wal->>$8, $9) as columns ...
FROM realtime.list_changes($1, $2, $3, $4)
```

**Problem:** 38,433 total calls extracting JSON fields with ->> operator repeatedly.

**Solutions:**
1. **Reduce realtime subscription frequency** - Current polling is excessive
2. **Batch subscriptions** - Combine multiple table subscriptions into fewer calls
3. **Materialize JSON fields** - Add indexed columns for frequently accessed fields
4. **Client-side caching** - Cache results for 1-5 seconds to reduce calls
5. **Review subscription filters** - Ensure clients only subscribe to needed data
6. **Connection pooling** - Use connection pooler to reduce overhead
7. **Consider alternatives** - For non-critical updates, use webhooks or scheduled fetches

**Expected impact:** 80-90% reduction in query time if subscriptions reduced by half

## 2. pg_timezone_names (8% of DB time)
**122 calls, 19 seconds total**
```sql
SELECT name FROM pg_timezone_names
```

**Fix:** Cache result at application startup. Timezone names never change. Return static list instead of querying.

## 3. Table Definition Generation (2-3s total)
**6+ queries using pg_temp.pg_get_tabledef, each 600-680ms**

**Fixes:**
- Cache generated table definitions (they rarely change)
- Regenerate only on schema changes
- Use application-level caching with 5-15 min TTL

## 4. Metadata Catalog Queries (3-5s total)
Multiple complex queries fetching pg_catalog data for dashboard/API:
- Base types recursive CTE: 122 calls, 3.3s
- Table/column metadata: Multiple 1-2s queries
- Function metadata: 6 calls, 1.2s

**Fixes:**
- Implement result caching with 5-15 min TTL
- Only refresh when schema changes detected
- Use pg_stat_statements to detect schema modifications

## 5. Miscellaneous Overhead
- PGMQ maintenance: 12 calls, 575ms
- Index creation: 417ms
